# facett-form 0.1.10 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/facett-form/0.1.10

**facett-form** — administrative / CRUD forms as a [`Facet`]. A consumer
implements [`FormModel`] for its record struct `T`; [`FormView<T>`] drives it:
labelled fields (text / multiline / number / select-enum / masked date /
checkbox), **per-field validation + red-outline error styling** (delegated to
[`egui_form`] backed by [`garde`]), sections, submit / reset, and
**dirty-tracking** against a baseline snapshot.

The hard part — turning a validation report into per-field error outlines and
messages — is *not* re-solved here: it's `egui_form`'s, wrapped behind a thin
[`FormUi`] field-builder so consumers never touch `egui_form` directly and the
backend stays swappable (see `.nornir/design/facett-form.md`).

Clipboard: a field's own Ctrl-C/V inside a `TextEdit` is egui-native; the
**facet-level** [`Facet::copy`]/[`Facet::paste`] round-trips the *whole model*
as JSON via [`FormModel::to_clip`]/[`FormModel::from_clip`].

---

# egui_form - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/egui_form/^0.8/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#egui_form)egui_form

egui_form adds form validation to egui.
It can either use [validator](https://crates.io/crates/validator)
or [garde](https://crates.io/crates/garde) for validation.
This also means, if you use rust you can use the same validation logic
on the server and the client.

Check the docs for the [validator implementation](https://docs.rs/egui_form/latest/egui_form/validator/index.html)
or the [garde implementation](https://docs.rs/egui_form/latest/egui_form/garde/index.html)
to get started.

You can also build a custom implementation by implementing the `EguiValidationReport` for the result of whatever
form validation crate you use.

[§](https://docs.rs#showcase)Showcase

You can [try the Signup Form example](https://lucasmerlin.github.io/hello_egui/#/example/signup_form) in hello_egui
showcase app.

Also, here’s a screenshot from HelloPaint’s profile form:

[§](https://docs.rs#should-i-use-validator-or-garde)Should I use validator or garde?

For small / prototype projects, I’d recommend garde, since it has built in error messages. For bigger projects that might require i18n, it might make sense to use validator, since it allows for custom error messages (garde as of now has no i18n support).

In HelloPaint I’m using garde, since it seems a bit cleaner and more active, hoping that i18n will be solved before it becomes a problem for HelloPaint.

[§](https://docs.rs#minimal-example-using-garde)Minimal example using garde

From [egui_form_minimal.rs](https://github.com/lucasmerlin/hello_egui/blob/main/crates/egui_form/examples/egui_form_minimal.rs)

```
use eframe::NativeOptions;
use egui::{TextEdit, Ui};
use egui_form::garde::{GardeReport, field_path};
use egui_form::{Form, FormField};
use garde::Validate;
#[derive(Debug, Default, Validate)]
struct Fields {
    #[garde(length(min = 2, max = 50))]
    user_name: String,
}
fn form_ui(ui: &mut Ui, fields: &mut Fields) {
    let mut form = Form::new().add_report(GardeReport::new(fields.validate()));
    FormField::new(&mut form, field_path!("user_name"))
        .label("User Name")
        .ui(ui, TextEdit::singleline(&mut fields.user_name));
    if let Some(Ok(())) = form.handle_submit(&ui.button("Submit"), ui) {
        println!("Submitted: {:?}", fields);
    }
}
```
## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [garde](https://docs.rs/garde/index.html)
- To use [garde](https://docs.rs/garde/index.html)with`egui_form`, you need to create a`garde::GardeReport`[Form](https://docs.rs/struct.Form.html)instance.
- [validator](https://docs.rs/validator/index.html)
- To use [validator](https://docs.rs/validator/index.html)with`egui_form`, you need to create a`validator::ValidatorReport`[Form](https://docs.rs/struct.Form.html)instance.

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [_garde_](https://docs.rs/macro._garde_field_path.html)- field_ - path
- Create a `garde::Path``crate::FormField::new`
- [_validator_](https://docs.rs/macro._validator_field_path.html)- field_ - path
- Create a field path to be submitted to a `crate::FormField::new``PathItem`

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Form](https://docs.rs/struct.Form.html)
- Form connects the state of the individual form fields with the validation results. It’s also responsible for handling the submission and focusing the first invalid field on error.
- [Form](https://docs.rs/struct.FormField.html)- Field
- A form field that can be validated.
Will color the field red (using the color from `egui::style::Visuals::error_fg_color`

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Egui](https://docs.rs/trait.EguiValidationReport.html)- Validation - Report
- A trait telling `egui_form`how to parse validation errors.
- [Into](https://docs.rs/trait.IntoFieldPath.html)- Field - Path
- Helper trait to allow constructing non-nested `FormFields`without using the`field_path`!() macro

---

# garde - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/garde/^0.22/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#garde--documentation-latest-version)Garde

A Rust validation library

- [Basic usage example](https://docs.rs#basic-usage-example)
- [Validation rules](https://docs.rs#available-validation-rules)
- [Length modes](https://docs.rs#length-modes)
- [Inner type validation](https://docs.rs#inner-type-validation)
- [Newtypes](https://docs.rs#newtypes)
- [Handling Option](https://docs.rs#handling-option)
- [Custom validation](https://docs.rs#custom-validation)
- [Context/Self access](https://docs.rs#contextself-access)
- [Implementing rules](https://docs.rs#implementing-rules)
- [Implementing](https://docs.rs#implementing-validate)- `Validate`
- [Rule adapters](https://docs.rs#rule-adapters)
- [Integration with web frameworks](https://docs.rs#integration-with-web-frameworks)
- [Feature flags](https://docs.rs#feature-flags)
- [Why](https://docs.rs#why-garde)- `garde`?

[§](https://docs.rs#basic-usage-example)Basic usage example

To get started, install `garde`:

`cargo add garde -F full`And attach the `Validate` derive to your type. `garde` will generate an implementation of the `Validate` trait for you,
allowing you to call the `validate` method.

Here’s what that looks like in full:

```
use garde::{Validate, Valid};
#[derive(Validate)]
struct User<'a> {
    #[garde(ascii, length(min=3, max=25))]
    username: &'a str,
    #[garde(length(min=15))]
    password: &'a str,
}
let user = User {
    username: "test",
    password: "not_a_very_good_password",
};
if let Err(e) = user.validate() {
    println!("invalid user: {e}");
}
```
Garde can also validate enums:

```
use garde::{Validate, Valid};
#[derive(Validate)]
enum Data {
    Struct {
        #[garde(range(min=-10, max=10))]
        field: i32,
    },
    Tuple(
        #[garde(ascii)]
        String
    ),
}
let data = Data::Struct { field: 100 };
if let Err(e) = data.validate() {
    println!("invalid data: {e}");
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#available-validation-rules)Available validation rules

| name | format | validation | feature flag |
|---|---|---|---|
| required | `#[garde(required)]` | is value set | - |
| ascii | `#[garde(ascii)]` | only contains ASCII | - |
| alphanumeric | `#[garde(alphanumeric)]` | only letters and digits | - |
| `#[garde(email)]` | an email according to the HTML5 spec [1](https://docs.rs#fn1) | `email` | |
| url | `#[garde(url)]` | a URL | `url` |
| ip | `#[garde(ip)]` | an IP address (either IPv4 or IPv6) | - |
| ipv4 | `#[garde(ipv4)]` | an IPv4 address | - |
| ipv6 | `#[garde(ipv6)]` | an IPv6 address | - |
| credit card | `#[garde(credit_card)]` | a credit card number | `credit-card` |
| phone number | `#[garde(phone_number)]` | a phone number | `phone-number` |
| length | `#[garde(length(<mode>, min=<usize>, max=<usize>, equal=<usize>)]` | a container with length in `min..=max`or`equal` | - |
| matches | `#[garde(matches(<field>))]` | a field matches another field | - |
| range | `#[garde(range(min=<expr>, max=<expr>, equal=<expr>))]` | a number in the range `min..=max`or`equal` | - |
| contains | `#[garde(contains(<string>))]` | a string-like value containing a substring | - |
| prefix | `#[garde(prefix(<string>))]` | a string-like value prefixed by some string | - |
| suffix | `#[garde(suffix(<string>))]` | a string-like value suffixed by some string | - |
| pattern | `#[garde(pattern("<regex>"))]` | a string-like value matching some regular expression | `regex` |
| pattern | `#[garde(pattern(<matcher>))]` | a string-like value matched by some [Matcher](https://docs.rs/garde/latest/garde/rules/pattern/trait.Matcher.html) | - |
| dive | `#[garde(dive)]` | nested validation, calls `validate`on the value | - |
| skip | `#[garde(skip)]` | skip validation | - |
| custom | `#[garde(custom(<function or closure>))]` | a custom validator | - |

Additional notes:

- `required`is only available for- `Option`fields.
- `dive`accepts an optional context:- `#[garde(dive(self.other_field))]`
- The `<mode>`argument for`length`is[explained here](https://docs.rs#length-modes)
- For `length`and`range`:- If `equal`is defined,`min`and`max`must be omitted.
- Assuming `equal`is omitted, either`min`or`max`may be omitted, but not both.
- `min`and- `max`use an- *inclusive*upper bound (- `min..=max`). Setting- `min == max`is equivalent to using- `equal`.

- If
- For `contains`,`prefix`, and`suffix`, the pattern must be a string literal, because the`Pattern`API[is currently unstable](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/issues/27721).
- Garde does not enable the default features of the `regex`crate - if you need extra regex features (e.g. Unicode) or better performance, add a dependency on`regex = "1"`to your`Cargo.toml`.

If most of the fields on your struct are annotated with `#[garde(skip)]`, you may use `#[garde(allow_unvalidated)]` instead:

```
#[derive(garde::Validate)]
struct Foo<'a> {
    #[garde(length(min = 1))]
    a: &'a str,
    #[garde(skip)]
    b: &'a str, // this field will not be validated
}
#[derive(garde::Validate)]
#[garde(allow_unvalidated)]
struct Bar<'a> {
    #[garde(length(min = 1))]
    a: &'a str,
    b: &'a str, // this field will not be validated
                // note the lack of `#[garde(skip)]`
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#length-modes)Length modes

The `length` rule accepts an optional `mode` argument, which determines what *kind* of length it will validate.

The options are:

- `simple`
- `bytes`
- `graphemes`
- `utf16`
- `chars`

The `simple` is the default used when the `mode` argument is omitted. The meaning of “simple length”
depends on the type. It is currently implemented for strings, where it validates the number of bytes,
and `std::collections`, where it validates the number of items.

```
#[derive(garde::Validate)]
struct Foo {
    #[garde(length(min = 1, max = 100))]
    string: String,
    #[garde(length(min = 1, max = 100))]
    collection: Vec<u32>
}
```
The `bytes`, `graphemes`, `utf16`, and `chars` exist mostly for string validation:

- `bytes`validates the number of- *bytes*
- `graphemens`uses the- `unicode-segmentation`- *graphemes*
- `utf16`uses- `encode_utf16`- *code points*
- `chars`uses- `chars`- *unicode scalar values*

```
#[derive(garde::Validate)]
struct Foo {
    #[garde(length(bytes, min = 1, max = 100))]
    a: String, // `a.len()`

    #[garde(length(graphemes, min = 1, max = 100))]
    b: String, // `b.graphemes().count()`

    #[garde(length(utf16, min = 1, max = 100))]
    c: String, // `c.encode_utf16().count()`

    #[garde(length(chars, min = 1, max = 100))]
    d: String, // `d.chars().count()`
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#inner-type-validation)Inner type validation

If you need to validate the “inner” type of a container, such as the `String` in `Vec<String>`, then use the `inner` modifier:

```
#[derive(garde::Validate)]
struct Test {
    #[garde(
        length(min = 1),
        inner(ascii, length(min = 1)), // wrap the rule in `inner`
    )]
    items: Vec<String>,
}
```
The above type would fail validation if:

- the `Vec`is empty
- any of the inner `String`elements is empty
- any of the inner `String`elements contains non-ASCII characters

To validate a deeply-nested type, such as `Vec<Option<String>>`, the `inner` modifier must be nested for each level of generics:

```
#[derive(garde::Validate)]
struct Test {
    #[garde(
        length(min = 1), // applies to `Vec`
        inner(inner(ascii, length(min = 1))), // applies to `String`
    )]
    items: Vec<Option<String>>,
}
```
You can apply separate rules to every level of the nested type:

```
#[derive(garde::Validate)]
struct Test {
    #[garde(
        length(min = 1), // applies to `Vec`
        inner(required), // applies to `Option`
        inner(inner(ascii, length(min = 1))), // applies to `String`
    )]
    items: Vec<Option<String>>,
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#newtypes)Newtypes

The best way to re-use validation rules on a field is to use the [newtype idiom](https://doc.rust-lang.org/rust-by-example/generics/new_types.html)
with `#[garde(transparent)]`:

```
#[derive(garde::Validate)]
#[garde(transparent)]
struct Username(#[garde(length(min = 3, max = 20))] String);
#[derive(garde::Validate)]
struct User {
    // later used with `dive`:
    #[garde(dive)]
    username: Username,
}
```
The `username` field in the above example will inherit all the validation rules from the `String` field on `Username`. The result is that the error path will be flattened by one level, resulting in cleaner error messages:

Without the `#[garde(transparent)]` attribute, it would instead be:

Structs with the `#[garde(transparent)]` attribute may have more than one field, but there must be only one unskipped field. That means every field other than the one you wish to validate must be `#[garde(skip)]`.

[§](https://docs.rs#handling-option)Handling Option

Every rule works on `Option<T>` fields. The field will only be validated if it is `Some`. If you additionally want to validate that the `Option<T>` field is `Some`, use the `required` rule:

```
#[derive(garde::Validate)]
struct Test {
    #[garde(required, ascii, length(min = 1))]
    value: Option<String>,
}
```
The above type would fail validation if:

- `value`is- `None`
- the inner `value`is empty
- the inner `value`contains non-ASCII characters

[§](https://docs.rs#custom-validation)Custom validation

Validation may be customized via the `custom` rule, and the `context` attribute.

The context may be any type without generic parameters. By default, the context is `()`.

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
#[derive(garde::Validate)]
#[garde(context(PasswordContext))]
struct User {
    #[garde(custom(is_strong_password))]
    password: String,
}
struct PasswordContext {
    min_entropy: f32,
    entropy: cracken::password_entropy::EntropyEstimator,
}
fn is_strong_password(value: &str, context: &PasswordContext) -> garde::Result {
    let bits = context.entropy.estimate_password_entropy(value.as_bytes())
        .map(|e| e.mask_entropy)
        .unwrap_or(0.0);
    if bits < context.min_entropy {
        return Err(garde::Error::new("password is not strong enough"));
    }
    Ok(())
}
let ctx = PasswordContext { /* ... */ };
let user = User { /* ... */ };
user.validate(&ctx)?;
```
The validator function may accept the value as a reference to any type which it derefs to.
In the above example, it is possible to use `&str`, because `password` is a `String`, and `String` derefs to `&str`.

The `#[garde(custom(...))]` attribute accepts any expression which evalutes to a something which implements the following trait:

That means it’s possible to use higher order functions:

```
// Returns a function which does the actual validation.
fn my_equals(other: &str) -> impl FnOnce(&str, &()) -> garde::Result + '_ {
    move |value, _| {
        if value != other {
            return Err(garde::Error::new(format!("not equal to {other}")));
        }
        Ok(())
    }
}
#[derive(garde::Validate)]
struct User {
    #[garde(length(min = 1, max = 255))]
    password: String,
    // Combined with `self` access in rules:
    #[garde(custom(my_equals(&self.password2)))]
    password2: String,
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#contextself-access)Context/Self access

It’s generally possible to also access the context and `self`, because they are in scope in the output of the proc macro:

```
struct Limits {
    min: usize,
    max: usize,
}
struct Config {
    username: Limits,
}
#[derive(garde::Validate)]
#[garde(context(Config as ctx))]
struct User {
    #[garde(length(min = ctx.username.min, max = ctx.username.max))]
    username: String,
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#implementing-rules)Implementing rules

Say you want to implement length checking for a custom string-like type.
To do this, you would implement one of the `length` traits for it, depending
on what kind of validation you are looking for.

```
#[repr(transparent)]
pub struct MyString(String);
impl garde::rules::length::HasSimpleLength for MyString {
    fn length(&self) -> usize {
        self.0.len()
    }
}
#[derive(garde::Validate)]
struct Foo {
    // Now the `length` check may be used with `MyString`
    #[garde(length(min = 1, max = 1000))]
    field: MyString,
}
```
Each rule comes with its own trait that may be implemented by custom types in your code.
They are all available under `garde::rules`.

[§](https://docs.rs#implementing-validate)Implementing `Validate`

In case you have a container type for which you’d like to support nested validation (using the `#[garde(dive)]` rule),
you may implement `Validate` for it:

```
#[repr(transparent)]
struct MyVec<T>(Vec<T>);
impl<T: garde::Validate> garde::Validate for MyVec<T> {
    type Context = T::Context;
    fn validate_into(
        &self,
        ctx: &Self::Context,
        mut parent: &mut dyn FnMut() -> garde::Path,
        report: &mut garde::Report
    ) {
        for (index, item) in self.0.iter().enumerate() {
            let mut path = garde::util::nested_path!(parent, index);
            item.validate_into(ctx, &mut path, report);
        }
    }
}
#[derive(garde::Validate)]
struct Foo {
  #[garde(dive)]
  field: MyVec<Bar>,
}
#[derive(garde::Validate)]
struct Bar {
  #[garde(range(min = 1, max = 10))]
  value: u32,
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#rule-adapters)Rule adapters

Adapters allow you to implement validation for third-party types without using a newtype.

An adapter may look like this:

```
mod my_str_adapter {
    #![allow(unused_imports)]
    pub use garde::rules::*; // re-export garde's rules
    pub mod length {
        pub use garde::rules::length::*; // re-export `length` rules
        pub mod simple {
            // re-implement `simple`, but _only_ for the concrete type &str!
            pub fn apply(v: &str, (min, max): (usize, usize)) -> garde::Result {
                if !(min..=max).contains(&v.len()) {
                    Err(garde::Error::new("my custom error message"))
                } else {
                    Ok(())
                }
            }
        }
    }
}
```
You create a module, add a public glob re-export of `garde::rules` inside of it,
and then re-implement the specific rule you’re interested in. This is a form of
[duck typing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duck_typing). Any rule which you have
not re-implemented is simply delegated to `garde`’s impl.

It’s quite verbose, but in exchange it is maximally flexible. To use the adapter,
add an `adapt` attribute to a field:

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
#[derive(garde::Validate)]
struct Stuff<'a> {
    #[garde(
        adapt(my_str_adapter),
        length(min = 1),
        ascii,
    )]
    v: &'a str,
}
```
The `length` rule will now use your custom implementation, but the `ascii` rule
will continue to use `garde`’s implementation.

[§](https://docs.rs#integration-with-web-frameworks)Integration with web frameworks

[§](https://docs.rs#feature-flags)Feature flags

| name | description | extra dependencies |
|---|---|---|
| `derive` | Enables the usage of the `derive(Validate)`macro | `garde_derive` |
| `url` | Validation of URLs via the `url`crate. | `url` |
| `email` | Validation of emails according to [HTML5](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/forms.html#valid-e-mail-address) | ,`regex``once_cell` |
| `email-idna` | Support for [Internationalizing Domain Names for Applications](https://url.spec.whatwg.org/#idna)in email addresses | `idna` |
| `regex` | Support for regular expressions in `pattern`via the`regex`crate | ,`regex``once_cell` |
| `credit-card` | Validation of credit card numbers via the `card-validate`crate | `card-validate` |
| `phone-number` | Validation of phone numbers via the `phonenumber`crate | `phonenumber` |
| `unicode` | Validation of grapheme count via the `unicode-segmentation`crate | `unicode-segmentation` |

[§](https://docs.rs#why-garde)Why `garde`?

Garde means guard in French. I am not French, nor do I speak the language, but `guard` was taken, and this is close enough :).

# facett_form - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/facett-form/0.1.10/target-redirect/facett_form/

## Expand description

**facett-form** — administrative / CRUD forms as a [ Facet](https://docs.rs/facett-core/0.1.10/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/facett_core/trait.Facet.html). A consumer
implements

[for its record struct](https://docs.rs/trait.FormModel.html)

`FormModel``T`; [drives it: labelled fields (text / multiline / number / select-enum / masked date / checkbox),](https://docs.rs/struct.FormView.html)

`FormView<T>`**per-field validation + red-outline error styling**(delegated to

[backed by](https://docs.rs/egui_form/0.8.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/egui_form/index.html)

`egui_form`[), sections, submit / reset, and](https://docs.rs/garde/0.22.1/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/garde/index.html)

`garde`**dirty-tracking**against a baseline snapshot.

The hard part — turning a validation report into per-field error outlines and
messages — is *not* re-solved here: it’s `egui_form`’s, wrapped behind a thin
[ FormUi](https://docs.rs/struct.FormUi.html) field-builder so consumers never touch

`egui_form` directly and the
backend stays swappable (see `.nornir/design/facett-form.md`).Clipboard: a field’s own Ctrl-C/V inside a `TextEdit` is egui-native; the
**facet-level** [ Facet::copy](https://docs.rs/facett-core/0.1.10/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/facett_core/trait.Facet.html#method.copy)/

[round-trips the](https://docs.rs/facett-core/0.1.10/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/facett_core/trait.Facet.html#method.paste)

`Facet::paste`*whole model*as JSON via

[/](https://docs.rs/trait.FormModel.html#method.to_clip)

`FormModel::to_clip`[.](https://docs.rs/trait.FormModel.html#method.from_clip)

`FormModel::from_clip`## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [FormUi](https://docs.rs/struct.FormUi.html)
- The per-frame field builder handed to `FormModel::fields``egui::Ui`and the`egui_form``Form`
- [Form](https://docs.rs/struct.FormView.html)- View
- The `Facet``T`, a baseline snapshot (for dirty-tracking
- [Validation](https://docs.rs/struct.ValidationReport.html)- Report
- The validation report handed to `FormView``egui_form`’s`GardeReport``ValidationReport::ok``ValidationReport::from_garde``garde::Validate::validate`result).

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Form](https://docs.rs/trait.FormModel.html)- Model
- Implemented by the consumer’s record model: describe its fields + (optionally)
validate and serialize. `Clone + PartialEq`powers dirty-tracking and reset.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [valid_](https://docs.rs/fn.valid_ymd.html)- ymd
- Validate `YYYY-MM-DD`cheaply (no date crate): four-digit year, 01–12 month, 01–31 day (day-in-month not range-checked beyond 31). Handy as a garde`#[garde(custom(facett_form::valid_ymd))]`rule for`FormUi::date`

# lib.rs - source

# facett_form/lib.rs

[1](https://docs.rs#1)//! **facett-form** — administrative / CRUD forms as a [`Facet`]. A consumer
[2](https://docs.rs#2)//! implements [`FormModel`] for its record struct `T`; [`FormView<T>`] drives it:
[3](https://docs.rs#3)//! labelled fields (text / multiline / number / select-enum / masked date /
[4](https://docs.rs#4)//! checkbox), **per-field validation + red-outline error styling** (delegated to
[5](https://docs.rs#5)//! [`egui_form`] backed by [`garde`]), sections, submit / reset, and
[6](https://docs.rs#6)//! **dirty-tracking** against a baseline snapshot.
[7](https://docs.rs#7)//!
[8](https://docs.rs#8)//! The hard part — turning a validation report into per-field error outlines and
[9](https://docs.rs#9)//! messages — is *not* re-solved here: it's `egui_form`'s, wrapped behind a thin
[10](https://docs.rs#10)//! [`FormUi`] field-builder so consumers never touch `egui_form` directly and the
[11](https://docs.rs#11)//! backend stays swappable (see `.nornir/design/facett-form.md`).
[12](https://docs.rs#12)//!
[13](https://docs.rs#13)//! Clipboard: a field's own Ctrl-C/V inside a `TextEdit` is egui-native; the
[14](https://docs.rs#14)//! **facet-level** [`Facet::copy`]/[`Facet::paste`] round-trips the *whole model*
[15](https://docs.rs#15)//! as JSON via [`FormModel::to_clip`]/[`FormModel::from_clip`].
[16](https://docs.rs#16)
[17](https://docs.rs#17)use egui::Ui;
[18](https://docs.rs#18)use egui_form::garde::GardeReport;
[19](https://docs.rs#19)use egui_form::{Form, FormField};
[20](https://docs.rs#20)use facett_core::clip::{ClipKind, ClipPayload, CopySource, PasteTarget};
[21](https://docs.rs#21)use facett_core::{Facet, FacetCaps, theme};
[22](https://docs.rs#22)
[23](https://docs.rs#23)/// The validation report handed to [`FormView`]: a thin wrapper over
[24](https://docs.rs#24)/// `egui_form`'s [`GardeReport`], so the backend stays behind facett's seam.
[25](https://docs.rs#25)/// Build one with [`ValidationReport::ok`] (no errors) or
[26](https://docs.rs#26)/// [`ValidationReport::from_garde`] (from a `garde::Validate::validate` result).
[27](https://docs.rs#27)#[derive(Default)]
[28](https://docs.rs#28)pub struct ValidationReport {
[29](https://docs.rs#29)    /// `field path -> message`, extracted once so we can both seed `egui_form`'s
[30](https://docs.rs#30)    /// per-field outlines and surface a `state_json` errors map for headless tests.
[31](https://docs.rs#31)    errors: Vec<(String, String)>,
[32](https://docs.rs#32)}
[33](https://docs.rs#33)
[34](https://docs.rs#34)impl ValidationReport {
[35](https://docs.rs#35)    /// An empty (valid) report.
[36](https://docs.rs#36)    pub fn ok() -> Self {
[37](https://docs.rs#37)        Self { errors: Vec::new() }
[38](https://docs.rs#38)    }
[39](https://docs.rs#39)
[40](https://docs.rs#40)    /// Build from a `garde::Validate::validate()` result. `Ok(())` → no errors;
[41](https://docs.rs#41)    /// `Err(report)` → one entry per offending field path.
[42](https://docs.rs#42)    pub fn from_garde(result: Result<(), garde::Report>) -> Self {
[43](https://docs.rs#43)        let mut errors = Vec::new();
[44](https://docs.rs#44)        if let Err(report) = &result {
[45](https://docs.rs#45)            for (path, err) in report.iter() {
[46](https://docs.rs#46)                errors.push((path.to_string(), err.to_string()));
[47](https://docs.rs#47)            }
[48](https://docs.rs#48)        }
[49](https://docs.rs#49)        Self { errors }
[50](https://docs.rs#50)    }
[51](https://docs.rs#51)
[52](https://docs.rs#52)    /// True when there are no validation errors.
[53](https://docs.rs#53)    pub fn is_empty(&self) -> bool {
[54](https://docs.rs#54)        self.errors.is_empty()
[55](https://docs.rs#55)    }
[56](https://docs.rs#56)
[57](https://docs.rs#57)    /// Number of field errors.
[58](https://docs.rs#58)    pub fn len(&self) -> usize {
[59](https://docs.rs#59)        self.errors.len()
[60](https://docs.rs#60)    }
[61](https://docs.rs#61)
[62](https://docs.rs#62)    /// The message for a specific field id, if any.
[63](https://docs.rs#63)    pub fn field_error(&self, id: &str) -> Option<&str> {
[64](https://docs.rs#64)        self.errors.iter().find(|(p, _)| p == id).map(|(_, m)| m.as_str())
[65](https://docs.rs#65)    }
[66](https://docs.rs#66)
[67](https://docs.rs#67)    /// `{ field_id: message, … }` — folded into the facet's `state_json` so
[68](https://docs.rs#68)    /// headless tests can assert exactly which fields are invalid.
[69](https://docs.rs#69)    pub fn to_json(&self) -> serde_json::Value {
[70](https://docs.rs#70)        let mut map = serde_json::Map::new();
[71](https://docs.rs#71)        for (path, msg) in &self.errors {
[72](https://docs.rs#72)            map.insert(path.clone(), serde_json::Value::String(msg.clone()));
[73](https://docs.rs#73)        }
[74](https://docs.rs#74)        serde_json::Value::Object(map)
[75](https://docs.rs#75)    }
[76](https://docs.rs#76)}
[77](https://docs.rs#77)
[78](https://docs.rs#78)/// Implemented by the consumer's record model: describe its fields + (optionally)
[79](https://docs.rs#79)/// validate and serialize. `Clone + PartialEq` powers dirty-tracking and reset.
[80](https://docs.rs#80)pub trait FormModel: Clone + PartialEq {
[81](https://docs.rs#81)    /// Lay the fields out into `form`. Called each frame (and once headlessly to
[82](https://docs.rs#82)    /// build the validation report). Read/write `&mut self`'s fields here.
[83](https://docs.rs#83)    fn fields(&mut self, form: &mut FormUi<'_>);
[84](https://docs.rs#84)
[85](https://docs.rs#85)    /// Validate; return a report keyed by field id. Default: always ok. Typically
[86](https://docs.rs#86)    /// `ValidationReport::from_garde(self.validate())` with `#[derive(garde::Validate)]`.
[87](https://docs.rs#87)    fn validate(&self) -> ValidationReport {
[88](https://docs.rs#88)        ValidationReport::ok()
[89](https://docs.rs#89)    }
[90](https://docs.rs#90)
[91](https://docs.rs#91)    /// Serialize to text for the facet-level clipboard copy (default: empty).
[92](https://docs.rs#92)    /// Typically `serde_json::to_string_pretty(self)`.
[93](https://docs.rs#93)    fn to_clip(&self) -> String {
[94](https://docs.rs#94)        String::new()
[95](https://docs.rs#95)    }
[96](https://docs.rs#96)
[97](https://docs.rs#97)    /// Hydrate from pasted text (default: no-op). Return true if applied.
[98](https://docs.rs#98)    /// Typically `serde_json::from_str(text).map(|m| *self = m).is_ok()`.
[99](https://docs.rs#99)    // Name + `&mut self` are intentional (the inverse of `to_clip`; mutates in
[100](https://docs.rs#100)    // place from a clipboard payload) — not a constructor, so the from_* lint
[101](https://docs.rs#101)    // doesn't apply here.
[102](https://docs.rs#102)    #[allow(clippy::wrong_self_convention)]
[103](https://docs.rs#103)    fn from_clip(&mut self, _text: &str) -> bool {
[104](https://docs.rs#104)        false
[105](https://docs.rs#105)    }
[106](https://docs.rs#106)}
[107](https://docs.rs#107)
[108](https://docs.rs#108)/// The per-frame field builder handed to [`FormModel::fields`]. Wraps the
[109](https://docs.rs#109)/// `egui::Ui` and the `egui_form` [`Form`] (carrying the validation report), so
[110](https://docs.rs#110)/// every widget renders with the right label and per-field error outline.
[111](https://docs.rs#111)pub struct FormUi<'a> {
[112](https://docs.rs#112)    ui: &'a mut Ui,
[113](https://docs.rs#113)    form: Form<GardeReport>,
[114](https://docs.rs#114)}
[115](https://docs.rs#115)
[116](https://docs.rs#116)impl<'a> FormUi<'a> {
[117](https://docs.rs#117)    fn new(ui: &'a mut Ui, report: GardeReport) -> Self {
[118](https://docs.rs#118)        Self { ui, form: Form::new().add_report(report) }
[119](https://docs.rs#119)    }
[120](https://docs.rs#120)
[121](https://docs.rs#121)    /// A titled group of fields under a heading + separator. Field ids inside the
[122](https://docs.rs#122)    /// section share the form's single validation report.
[123](https://docs.rs#123)    pub fn section(&mut self, title: &str, body: impl FnOnce(&mut FormUi<'_>)) {
[124](https://docs.rs#124)        let th = theme(self.ui);
[125](https://docs.rs#125)        self.ui.add_space(4.0);
[126](https://docs.rs#126)        self.ui.colored_label(th.accent, egui::RichText::new(title).strong());
[127](https://docs.rs#127)        self.ui.separator();
[128](https://docs.rs#128)        // Re-borrow the Ui into a fresh FormUi *sharing the same Form* (move it out,
[129](https://docs.rs#129)        // run the body, move it back) so all field ids land in one report.
[130](https://docs.rs#130)        let form = std::mem::replace(&mut self.form, Form::new());
[131](https://docs.rs#131)        let mut inner = FormUi { ui: &mut *self.ui, form };
[132](https://docs.rs#132)        body(&mut inner);
[133](https://docs.rs#133)        self.form = inner.form;
[134](https://docs.rs#134)    }
[135](https://docs.rs#135)
[136](https://docs.rs#136)    /// Single-line text field.
[137](https://docs.rs#137)    pub fn text(&mut self, id: &str, label: &str, value: &mut String) {
[138](https://docs.rs#138)        FormField::new(&mut self.form, id)
[139](https://docs.rs#139)            .label(label)
[140](https://docs.rs#140)            .ui(self.ui, egui::TextEdit::singleline(value));
[141](https://docs.rs#141)    }
[142](https://docs.rs#142)
[143](https://docs.rs#143)    /// Multi-line text field.
[144](https://docs.rs#144)    pub fn multiline(&mut self, id: &str, label: &str, value: &mut String) {
[145](https://docs.rs#145)        FormField::new(&mut self.form, id)
[146](https://docs.rs#146)            .label(label)
[147](https://docs.rs#147)            .ui(self.ui, egui::TextEdit::multiline(value));
[148](https://docs.rs#148)    }
[149](https://docs.rs#149)
[150](https://docs.rs#150)    /// Integer field (a `DragValue`, optionally range-clamped).
[151](https://docs.rs#151)    pub fn number_i64(&mut self, id: &str, label: &str, value: &mut i64, range: Option<std::ops::RangeInclusive<i64>>) {
[152](https://docs.rs#152)        let mut dv = egui::DragValue::new(value);
[153](https://docs.rs#153)        if let Some(r) = range {
[154](https://docs.rs#154)            dv = dv.range(r);
[155](https://docs.rs#155)        }
[156](https://docs.rs#156)        FormField::new(&mut self.form, id).label(label).ui(self.ui, dv);
[157](https://docs.rs#157)    }
[158](https://docs.rs#158)
[159](https://docs.rs#159)    /// Float field (a `DragValue`, optionally range-clamped).
[160](https://docs.rs#160)    pub fn number_f64(&mut self, id: &str, label: &str, value: &mut f64, range: Option<std::ops::RangeInclusive<f64>>) {
[161](https://docs.rs#161)        let mut dv = egui::DragValue::new(value);
[162](https://docs.rs#162)        if let Some(r) = range {
[163](https://docs.rs#163)            dv = dv.range(r);
[164](https://docs.rs#164)        }
[165](https://docs.rs#165)        FormField::new(&mut self.form, id).label(label).ui(self.ui, dv);
[166](https://docs.rs#166)    }
[167](https://docs.rs#167)
[168](https://docs.rs#168)    /// Enum-style select via a `ComboBox` over `options`. The bound `value` is the
[169](https://docs.rs#169)    /// chosen string; an out-of-set value still renders (the host may validate it).
[170](https://docs.rs#170)    pub fn select(&mut self, id: &str, label: &str, value: &mut String, options: &[&str]) {
[171](https://docs.rs#171)        // ComboBox isn't a `Widget`, so paint label + combo directly (the field
[172](https://docs.rs#172)        // outline matters less for a closed set, but we still keep the layout).
[173](https://docs.rs#173)        let th = theme(self.ui);
[174](https://docs.rs#174)        self.ui.add_space(2.0);
[175](https://docs.rs#175)        self.ui.label(egui::RichText::new(label).color(th.text).size(13.0));
[176](https://docs.rs#176)        egui::ComboBox::from_id_salt(format!("facett_form_select_{id}"))
[177](https://docs.rs#177)            .selected_text(value.clone())
[178](https://docs.rs#178)            .show_ui(self.ui, |ui| {
[179](https://docs.rs#179)                for opt in options {
[180](https://docs.rs#180)                    ui.selectable_value(value, (*opt).to_string(), *opt);
[181](https://docs.rs#181)                }
[182](https://docs.rs#182)            });
[183](https://docs.rs#183)    }
[184](https://docs.rs#184)
[185](https://docs.rs#185)    /// A `YYYY-MM-DD` masked text date field (zero extra deps). Pair with a
[186](https://docs.rs#186)    /// `#[garde(custom(...))]` or `#[garde(pattern(...))]` rule to validate format.
[187](https://docs.rs#187)    pub fn date(&mut self, id: &str, label: &str, value: &mut String) {
[188](https://docs.rs#188)        FormField::new(&mut self.form, id)
[189](https://docs.rs#189)            .label(label)
[190](https://docs.rs#190)            .ui(self.ui, egui::TextEdit::singleline(value).hint_text("YYYY-MM-DD"));
[191](https://docs.rs#191)    }
[192](https://docs.rs#192)
[193](https://docs.rs#193)    /// Boolean checkbox.
[194](https://docs.rs#194)    pub fn checkbox(&mut self, id: &str, label: &str, value: &mut bool) {
[195](https://docs.rs#195)        FormField::new(&mut self.form, id).label("").ui(self.ui, egui::Checkbox::new(value, label));
[196](https://docs.rs#196)    }
[197](https://docs.rs#197)}
[198](https://docs.rs#198)
[199](https://docs.rs#199)/// Validate `YYYY-MM-DD` cheaply (no date crate): four-digit year, 01–12 month,
[200](https://docs.rs#200)/// 01–31 day (day-in-month not range-checked beyond 31). Handy as a garde
[201](https://docs.rs#201)/// `#[garde(custom(facett_form::valid_ymd))]` rule for [`FormUi::date`] fields.
[202](https://docs.rs#202)pub fn valid_ymd<C>(value: &str, _ctx: &C) -> garde::Result {
[203](https://docs.rs#203)    let bytes = value.as_bytes();
[204](https://docs.rs#204)    let shaped = bytes.len() == 10 && bytes[4] == b'-' && bytes[7] == b'-';
[205](https://docs.rs#205)    let digits_ok = |range: std::ops::Range<usize>| value[range].bytes().all(|b| b.is_ascii_digit());
[206](https://docs.rs#206)    if shaped && digits_ok(0..4) && digits_ok(5..7) && digits_ok(8..10) {
[207](https://docs.rs#207)        let m: u32 = value[5..7].parse().unwrap_or(0);
[208](https://docs.rs#208)        let d: u32 = value[8..10].parse().unwrap_or(0);
[209](https://docs.rs#209)        if (1..=12).contains(&m) && (1..=31).contains(&d) {
[210](https://docs.rs#210)            return Ok(());
[211](https://docs.rs#211)        }
[212](https://docs.rs#212)    }
[213](https://docs.rs#213)    Err(garde::Error::new("expected a date as YYYY-MM-DD"))
[214](https://docs.rs#214)}
[215](https://docs.rs#215)
[216](https://docs.rs#216)/// The [`Facet`] driver: owns a model `T`, a baseline snapshot (for dirty-tracking
[217](https://docs.rs#217)/// + reset), the last validation report, and the last valid submitted model.
[218](https://docs.rs#218)pub struct FormView<T: FormModel> {
[219](https://docs.rs#219)    /// Tab / heading label.
[220](https://docs.rs#220)    pub title: String,
[221](https://docs.rs#221)    model: T,
[222](https://docs.rs#222)    baseline: T,
[223](https://docs.rs#223)    last_report: ValidationReport,
[224](https://docs.rs#224)    submitted: Option<T>,
[225](https://docs.rs#225)}
[226](https://docs.rs#226)
[227](https://docs.rs#227)impl<T: FormModel> FormView<T> {
[228](https://docs.rs#228)    /// New form over `model`; the baseline (clean state) is `model.clone()`.
[229](https://docs.rs#229)    pub fn new(title: impl Into<String>, model: T) -> Self {
[230](https://docs.rs#230)        let baseline = model.clone();
[231](https://docs.rs#231)        let last_report = model.validate();
[232](https://docs.rs#232)        Self { title: title.into(), model, baseline, last_report, submitted: None }
[233](https://docs.rs#233)    }
[234](https://docs.rs#234)
[235](https://docs.rs#235)    /// True when the model differs from the baseline (drives the unsaved marker +
[236](https://docs.rs#236)    /// Save/Reset enablement).
[237](https://docs.rs#237)    pub fn is_dirty(&self) -> bool {
[238](https://docs.rs#238)        self.model != self.baseline
[239](https://docs.rs#239)    }
[240](https://docs.rs#240)
[241](https://docs.rs#241)    /// Whether the model currently validates clean.
[242](https://docs.rs#242)    pub fn is_valid(&self) -> bool {
[243](https://docs.rs#243)        self.last_report.is_empty()
[244](https://docs.rs#244)    }
[245](https://docs.rs#245)
[246](https://docs.rs#246)    /// Take the last valid submitted model, if any (the host pulls this to persist).
[247](https://docs.rs#247)    pub fn take_submitted(&mut self) -> Option<T> {
[248](https://docs.rs#248)        self.submitted.take()
[249](https://docs.rs#249)    }
[250](https://docs.rs#250)
[251](https://docs.rs#251)    /// Discard edits: `model = baseline`.
[252](https://docs.rs#252)    pub fn reset(&mut self) {
[253](https://docs.rs#253)        self.model = self.baseline.clone();
[254](https://docs.rs#254)        self.last_report = self.model.validate();
[255](https://docs.rs#255)    }
[256](https://docs.rs#256)
[257](https://docs.rs#257)    /// Borrow the current model.
[258](https://docs.rs#258)    pub fn model(&self) -> &T {
[259](https://docs.rs#259)        &self.model
[260](https://docs.rs#260)    }
[261](https://docs.rs#261)
[262](https://docs.rs#262)    /// Borrow the current model mutably (host-side programmatic edits; re-validates).
[263](https://docs.rs#263)    pub fn model_mut(&mut self) -> &mut T {
[264](https://docs.rs#264)        &mut self.model
[265](https://docs.rs#265)    }
[266](https://docs.rs#266)
[267](https://docs.rs#267)    /// Re-validate after a programmatic edit via [`model_mut`](Self::model_mut).
[268](https://docs.rs#268)    pub fn revalidate(&mut self) {
[269](https://docs.rs#269)        self.last_report = self.model.validate();
[270](https://docs.rs#270)    }
[271](https://docs.rs#271)
[272](https://docs.rs#272)    /// Mark the current model as the clean baseline (e.g. after the host persists).
[273](https://docs.rs#273)    pub fn mark_clean(&mut self) {
[274](https://docs.rs#274)        self.baseline = self.model.clone();
[275](https://docs.rs#275)    }
[276](https://docs.rs#276)}
[277](https://docs.rs#277)
[278](https://docs.rs#278)// ── typed copy/paste (§16) — the whole model as its clipboard Text (JSON) ──────
[279](https://docs.rs#279)impl<T: FormModel> CopySource for FormView<T> {
[280](https://docs.rs#280)    fn copy_kinds(&self) -> &[ClipKind] {
[281](https://docs.rs#281)        &[ClipKind::Text]
[282](https://docs.rs#282)    }
[283](https://docs.rs#283)    fn copy_payload(&self) -> Option<ClipPayload> {
[284](https://docs.rs#284)        let s = self.model.to_clip();
[285](https://docs.rs#285)        (!s.is_empty()).then_some(ClipPayload::Text(s))
[286](https://docs.rs#286)    }
[287](https://docs.rs#287)}
[288](https://docs.rs#288)
[289](https://docs.rs#289)impl<T: FormModel> PasteTarget for FormView<T> {
[290](https://docs.rs#290)    fn accepts(&self, k: ClipKind) -> bool {
[291](https://docs.rs#291)        matches!(k, ClipKind::Text)
[292](https://docs.rs#292)    }
[293](https://docs.rs#293)    fn paste_payload(&mut self, p: &ClipPayload) {
[294](https://docs.rs#294)        if self.model.from_clip(&p.as_text()) {
[295](https://docs.rs#295)            self.last_report = self.model.validate();
[296](https://docs.rs#296)        }
[297](https://docs.rs#297)    }
[298](https://docs.rs#298)}
[299](https://docs.rs#299)
[300](https://docs.rs#300)impl<T: FormModel> Facet for FormView<T> {
[301](https://docs.rs#301)    fn title(&self) -> &str {
[302](https://docs.rs#302)        &self.title
[303](https://docs.rs#303)    }
[304](https://docs.rs#304)
[305](https://docs.rs#305)    fn ui(&mut self, ui: &mut Ui) {
[306](https://docs.rs#306)        // Validate the live model, then build the field UI seeded with the report
[307](https://docs.rs#307)        // so egui_form paints per-field red outlines + messages on the offenders.
[308](https://docs.rs#308)        // We reconstruct a garde::Report from our ValidationReport so the outlined
[309](https://docs.rs#309)        // field ids line up exactly with `state_json`'s `errors` map — and the
[310](https://docs.rs#310)        // FormModel stays garde-agnostic (it owns where errors come from).
[311](https://docs.rs#311)        self.last_report = self.model.validate();
[312](https://docs.rs#312)        let report = GardeReport::new(garde_result_from(&self.last_report));
[313](https://docs.rs#313)        {
[314](https://docs.rs#314)            let mut fu = FormUi::new(ui, report);
[315](https://docs.rs#315)            self.model.fields(&mut fu);
[316](https://docs.rs#316)        }
[317](https://docs.rs#317)
[318](https://docs.rs#318)        ui.separator();
[319](https://docs.rs#319)        ui.horizontal(|ui| {
[320](https://docs.rs#320)            let can_save = self.is_valid() && self.is_dirty();
[321](https://docs.rs#321)            if ui.add_enabled(can_save, egui::Button::new("Save")).on_hover_text("Submit the valid form").clicked() {
[322](https://docs.rs#322)                self.submitted = Some(self.model.clone());
[323](https://docs.rs#323)                self.baseline = self.model.clone();
[324](https://docs.rs#324)            }
[325](https://docs.rs#325)            if ui.add_enabled(self.is_dirty(), egui::Button::new("Reset")).clicked() {
[326](https://docs.rs#326)                self.reset();
[327](https://docs.rs#327)            }
[328](https://docs.rs#328)            if self.is_dirty() {
[329](https://docs.rs#329)                let th = theme(ui);
[330](https://docs.rs#330)                ui.colored_label(th.accent, "● unsaved");
[331](https://docs.rs#331)            }
[332](https://docs.rs#332)            if !self.is_valid() {
[333](https://docs.rs#333)                let th = theme(ui);
[334](https://docs.rs#334)                ui.colored_label(th.text_dim, format!("{} field error(s)", self.last_report.len()));
[335](https://docs.rs#335)            }
[336](https://docs.rs#336)        });
[337](https://docs.rs#337)    }
[338](https://docs.rs#338)
[339](https://docs.rs#339)    fn state_json(&self) -> serde_json::Value {
[340](https://docs.rs#340)        serde_json::json!({
[341](https://docs.rs#341)            "title": self.title,
[342](https://docs.rs#342)            "dirty": self.is_dirty(),
[343](https://docs.rs#343)            "valid": self.is_valid(),
[344](https://docs.rs#344)            "errors": self.last_report.to_json(),
[345](https://docs.rs#345)            "submitted": self.submitted.is_some(),
[346](https://docs.rs#346)        })
[347](https://docs.rs#347)    }
[348](https://docs.rs#348)
[349](https://docs.rs#349)    fn caps(&self) -> FacetCaps {
[350](https://docs.rs#350)        FacetCaps::NONE.copyable().pasteable().cuttable().selectable().searchable().themeable()
[351](https://docs.rs#351)    }
[352](https://docs.rs#352)
[353](https://docs.rs#353)    fn selection_json(&self) -> serde_json::Value {
[354](https://docs.rs#354)        // The whole model is the "selection" for clipboard purposes.
[355](https://docs.rs#355)        serde_json::json!({ "dirty": self.is_dirty(), "valid": self.is_valid() })
[356](https://docs.rs#356)    }
[357](https://docs.rs#357)
[358](https://docs.rs#358)    /// Facet-level copy: the whole model as the consumer's clipboard text (JSON).
[359](https://docs.rs#359)    fn copy(&mut self) -> Option<String> {
[360](https://docs.rs#360)        let s = self.model.to_clip();
[361](https://docs.rs#361)        if s.is_empty() { None } else { Some(s) }
[362](https://docs.rs#362)    }
[363](https://docs.rs#363)
[364](https://docs.rs#364)    /// Cut on a form is a copy (a form isn't a deletable selection); never clears.
[365](https://docs.rs#365)    fn cut(&mut self) -> Option<String> {
[366](https://docs.rs#366)        self.copy()
[367](https://docs.rs#367)    }
[368](https://docs.rs#368)
[369](https://docs.rs#369)    /// Facet-level paste: fill the model from pasted text; re-validate on success.
[370](https://docs.rs#370)    fn paste(&mut self, text: &str) -> bool {
[371](https://docs.rs#371)        if self.model.from_clip(text) {
[372](https://docs.rs#372)            self.last_report = self.model.validate();
[373](https://docs.rs#373)            true
[374](https://docs.rs#374)        } else {
[375](https://docs.rs#375)            false
[376](https://docs.rs#376)        }
[377](https://docs.rs#377)    }
[378](https://docs.rs#378)}
[379](https://docs.rs#379)
[380](https://docs.rs#380)/// Reconstruct the `Result<(), garde::Report>` that `egui_form`'s [`GardeReport`]
[381](https://docs.rs#381)/// consumes, from our backend-neutral [`ValidationReport`]. This lets `egui_form`
[382](https://docs.rs#382)/// outline the exact field ids our `state_json` reports, while keeping
[383](https://docs.rs#383)/// [`FormModel`] garde-agnostic (it owns where its errors come from).
[384](https://docs.rs#384)fn garde_result_from(report: &ValidationReport) -> Result<(), garde::Report> {
[385](https://docs.rs#385)    if report.is_empty() {
[386](https://docs.rs#386)        return Ok(());
[387](https://docs.rs#387)    }
[388](https://docs.rs#388)    let mut gr = garde::Report::new();
[389](https://docs.rs#389)    for (path, msg) in report.errors.iter() {
[390](https://docs.rs#390)        gr.append(garde::Path::new(path.clone()), garde::Error::new(msg.clone()));
[391](https://docs.rs#391)    }
[392](https://docs.rs#392)    Err(gr)
[393](https://docs.rs#393)}

# garde - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/garde/0.22.1/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/garde/index.html

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#garde--documentation-latest-version)Garde

A Rust validation library

- [Basic usage example](https://docs.rs#basic-usage-example)
- [Validation rules](https://docs.rs#available-validation-rules)
- [Length modes](https://docs.rs#length-modes)
- [Inner type validation](https://docs.rs#inner-type-validation)
- [Newtypes](https://docs.rs#newtypes)

- [Custom validation](https://docs.rs#custom-validation)
- [Context/Self access](https://docs.rs#contextself-access)

- [Implementing](https://docs.rs#implementing-validate)- `Validate`
- [Rule adapters](https://docs.rs#rule-adapters)

- [Why](https://docs.rs#why-garde)- `garde`?

[§](https://docs.rs#basic-usage-example)Basic usage example

To get started, install `garde`:

`cargo add garde -F full`And attach the `Validate` derive to your type. `garde` will generate an implementation of the `Validate` trait for you,
allowing you to call the `validate` method.

Here’s what that looks like in full:

```
use garde::{Validate, Valid};
#[derive(Validate)]
struct User<'a> {
    #[garde(ascii, length(min=3, max=25))]
    username: &'a str,
    #[garde(length(min=15))]
    password: &'a str,
}
let user = User {
    username: "test",
    password: "not_a_very_good_password",
};
if let Err(e) = user.validate() {
    println!("invalid user: {e}");
}
```
Garde can also validate enums:

```
use garde::{Validate, Valid};
#[derive(Validate)]
enum Data {
    Struct {
        #[garde(range(min=-10, max=10))]
        field: i32,
    },
    Tuple(
        #[garde(ascii)]
        String
    ),
}
let data = Data::Struct { field: 100 };
if let Err(e) = data.validate() {
    println!("invalid data: {e}");
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#available-validation-rules)Available validation rules

| name | format | validation | feature flag |
|---|---|---|---|
| required | `#[garde(required)]` | is value set | - |
| ascii | `#[garde(ascii)]` | only contains ASCII | - |
| alphanumeric | `#[garde(alphanumeric)]` | only letters and digits | - |
| `#[garde(email)]` | an email according to the HTML5 spec [1](https://docs.rs#fn1) | `email` | |
| url | `#[garde(url)]` | a URL | `url` |
| ip | `#[garde(ip)]` | an IP address (either IPv4 or IPv6) | - |
| ipv4 | `#[garde(ipv4)]` | an IPv4 address | - |
| ipv6 | `#[garde(ipv6)]` | an IPv6 address | - |
| credit card | `#[garde(credit_card)]` | a credit card number | `credit-card` |
| phone number | `#[garde(phone_number)]` | a phone number | `phone-number` |
| length | `#[garde(length(<mode>, min=<usize>, max=<usize>, equal=<usize>)]` | a container with length in `min..=max`or`equal` | - |
| matches | `#[garde(matches(<field>))]` | a field matches another field | - |
| range | `#[garde(range(min=<expr>, max=<expr>, equal=<expr>))]` | a number in the range `min..=max`or`equal` | - |
| contains | `#[garde(contains(<string>))]` | a string-like value containing a substring | - |
| prefix | `#[garde(prefix(<string>))]` | a string-like value prefixed by some string | - |
| suffix | `#[garde(suffix(<string>))]` | a string-like value suffixed by some string | - |
| pattern | `#[garde(pattern("<regex>"))]` | a string-like value matching some regular expression | `regex` |
| pattern | `#[garde(pattern(<matcher>))]` | a string-like value matched by some [Matcher](https://docs.rs/garde/latest/garde/rules/pattern/trait.Matcher.html) | - |
| dive | `#[garde(dive)]` | nested validation, calls `validate`on the value | - |
| skip | `#[garde(skip)]` | skip validation | - |
| custom | `#[garde(custom(<function or closure>))]` | a custom validator | - |

Additional notes:

- `required`is only available for- `Option`fields.
- `dive`accepts an optional context:- `#[garde(dive(self.other_field))]`
- The `<mode>`argument for`length`is[explained here](https://docs.rs#length-modes)
- For `length`and`range`:- If `equal`is defined,`min`and`max`must be omitted.
- Assuming `equal`is omitted, either`min`or`max`may be omitted, but not both.
- `min`and- `max`use an- *inclusive*upper bound (- `min..=max`). Setting- `min == max`is equivalent to using- `equal`.

- If
- For `contains`,`prefix`, and`suffix`, the pattern must be a string literal, because the`Pattern`API[is currently unstable](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/issues/27721).
- Garde does not enable the default features of the `regex`crate - if you need extra regex features (e.g. Unicode) or better performance, add a dependency on`regex = "1"`to your`Cargo.toml`.

If most of the fields on your struct are annotated with `#[garde(skip)]`, you may use `#[garde(allow_unvalidated)]` instead:

```
#[derive(garde::Validate)]
struct Foo<'a> {
    #[garde(length(min = 1))]
    a: &'a str,
    #[garde(skip)]
    b: &'a str, // this field will not be validated
}
#[derive(garde::Validate)]
#[garde(allow_unvalidated)]
struct Bar<'a> {
    #[garde(length(min = 1))]
    a: &'a str,
    b: &'a str, // this field will not be validated
                // note the lack of `#[garde(skip)]`
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#length-modes)Length modes

The `length` rule accepts an optional `mode` argument, which determines what *kind* of length it will validate.

The options are:

- `simple`
- `bytes`
- `graphemes`
- `utf16`
- `chars`

The `simple` is the default used when the `mode` argument is omitted. The meaning of “simple length”
depends on the type. It is currently implemented for strings, where it validates the number of bytes,
and `std::collections`, where it validates the number of items.

```
#[derive(garde::Validate)]
struct Foo {
    #[garde(length(min = 1, max = 100))]
    string: String,
    #[garde(length(min = 1, max = 100))]
    collection: Vec<u32>
}
```
The `bytes`, `graphemes`, `utf16`, and `chars` exist mostly for string validation:

- `bytes`validates the number of- *bytes*
- `graphemens`uses the- `unicode-segmentation`- *graphemes*
- `utf16`uses- `encode_utf16`- *code points*
- `chars`uses- `chars`- *unicode scalar values*

```
#[derive(garde::Validate)]
struct Foo {
    #[garde(length(bytes, min = 1, max = 100))]
    a: String, // `a.len()`

    #[garde(length(graphemes, min = 1, max = 100))]
    b: String, // `b.graphemes().count()`

    #[garde(length(utf16, min = 1, max = 100))]
    c: String, // `c.encode_utf16().count()`

    #[garde(length(chars, min = 1, max = 100))]
    d: String, // `d.chars().count()`
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#inner-type-validation)Inner type validation

If you need to validate the “inner” type of a container, such as the `String` in `Vec<String>`, then use the `inner` modifier:

```
#[derive(garde::Validate)]
struct Test {
    #[garde(
        length(min = 1),
        inner(ascii, length(min = 1)), // wrap the rule in `inner`
    )]
    items: Vec<String>,
}
```
The above type would fail validation if:

- the `Vec`is empty
- any of the inner `String`elements is empty
- any of the inner `String`elements contains non-ASCII characters

To validate a deeply-nested type, such as `Vec<Option<String>>`, the `inner` modifier must be nested for each level of generics:

```
#[derive(garde::Validate)]
struct Test {
    #[garde(
        length(min = 1), // applies to `Vec`
        inner(inner(ascii, length(min = 1))), // applies to `String`
    )]
    items: Vec<Option<String>>,
}
```
You can apply separate rules to every level of the nested type:

```
#[derive(garde::Validate)]
struct Test {
    #[garde(
        length(min = 1), // applies to `Vec`
        inner(required), // applies to `Option`
        inner(inner(ascii, length(min = 1))), // applies to `String`
    )]
    items: Vec<Option<String>>,
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#newtypes)Newtypes

The best way to re-use validation rules on a field is to use the [newtype idiom](https://doc.rust-lang.org/rust-by-example/generics/new_types.html)
with `#[garde(transparent)]`:

```
#[derive(garde::Validate)]
#[garde(transparent)]
struct Username(#[garde(length(min = 3, max = 20))] String);
#[derive(garde::Validate)]
struct User {
    // later used with `dive`:
    #[garde(dive)]
    username: Username,
}
```
The `username` field in the above example will inherit all the validation rules from the `String` field on `Username`. The result is that the error path will be flattened by one level, resulting in cleaner error messages:

Without the `#[garde(transparent)]` attribute, it would instead be:

Structs with the `#[garde(transparent)]` attribute may have more than one field, but there must be only one unskipped field. That means every field other than the one you wish to validate must be `#[garde(skip)]`.

[§](https://docs.rs#handling-option)Handling Option

Every rule works on `Option<T>` fields. The field will only be validated if it is `Some`. If you additionally want to validate that the `Option<T>` field is `Some`, use the `required` rule:

```
#[derive(garde::Validate)]
struct Test {
    #[garde(required, ascii, length(min = 1))]
    value: Option<String>,
}
```
The above type would fail validation if:

- `value`is- `None`
- the inner `value`is empty
- the inner `value`contains non-ASCII characters

[§](https://docs.rs#custom-validation)Custom validation

Validation may be customized via the `custom` rule, and the `context` attribute.

The context may be any type without generic parameters. By default, the context is `()`.

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
#[derive(garde::Validate)]
#[garde(context(PasswordContext))]
struct User {
    #[garde(custom(is_strong_password))]
    password: String,
}
struct PasswordContext {
    min_entropy: f32,
    entropy: cracken::password_entropy::EntropyEstimator,
}
fn is_strong_password(value: &str, context: &PasswordContext) -> garde::Result {
    let bits = context.entropy.estimate_password_entropy(value.as_bytes())
        .map(|e| e.mask_entropy)
        .unwrap_or(0.0);
    if bits < context.min_entropy {
        return Err(garde::Error::new("password is not strong enough"));
    }
    Ok(())
}
let ctx = PasswordContext { /* ... */ };
let user = User { /* ... */ };
user.validate(&ctx)?;
```
The validator function may accept the value as a reference to any type which it derefs to.
In the above example, it is possible to use `&str`, because `password` is a `String`, and `String` derefs to `&str`.

The `#[garde(custom(...))]` attribute accepts any expression which evalutes to a something which implements the following trait:

That means it’s possible to use higher order functions:

```
// Returns a function which does the actual validation.
fn my_equals(other: &str) -> impl FnOnce(&str, &()) -> garde::Result + '_ {
    move |value, _| {
        if value != other {
            return Err(garde::Error::new(format!("not equal to {other}")));
        }
        Ok(())
    }
}
#[derive(garde::Validate)]
struct User {
    #[garde(length(min = 1, max = 255))]
    password: String,
    // Combined with `self` access in rules:
    #[garde(custom(my_equals(&self.password2)))]
    password2: String,
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#contextself-access)Context/Self access

It’s generally possible to also access the context and `self`, because they are in scope in the output of the proc macro:

```
struct Limits {
    min: usize,
    max: usize,
}
struct Config {
    username: Limits,
}
#[derive(garde::Validate)]
#[garde(context(Config as ctx))]
struct User {
    #[garde(length(min = ctx.username.min, max = ctx.username.max))]
    username: String,
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#implementing-rules)Implementing rules

Say you want to implement length checking for a custom string-like type.
To do this, you would implement one of the `length` traits for it, depending
on what kind of validation you are looking for.

```
#[repr(transparent)]
pub struct MyString(String);
impl garde::rules::length::HasSimpleLength for MyString {
    fn length(&self) -> usize {
        self.0.len()
    }
}
#[derive(garde::Validate)]
struct Foo {
    // Now the `length` check may be used with `MyString`
    #[garde(length(min = 1, max = 1000))]
    field: MyString,
}
```
Each rule comes with its own trait that may be implemented by custom types in your code.
They are all available under `garde::rules`.

[§](https://docs.rs#implementing-validate)Implementing `Validate`

In case you have a container type for which you’d like to support nested validation (using the `#[garde(dive)]` rule),
you may implement `Validate` for it:

```
#[repr(transparent)]
struct MyVec<T>(Vec<T>);
impl<T: garde::Validate> garde::Validate for MyVec<T> {
    type Context = T::Context;
    fn validate_into(
        &self,
        ctx: &Self::Context,
        mut parent: &mut dyn FnMut() -> garde::Path,
        report: &mut garde::Report
    ) {
        for (index, item) in self.0.iter().enumerate() {
            let mut path = garde::util::nested_path!(parent, index);
            item.validate_into(ctx, &mut path, report);
        }
    }
}
#[derive(garde::Validate)]
struct Foo {
  #[garde(dive)]
  field: MyVec<Bar>,
}
#[derive(garde::Validate)]
struct Bar {
  #[garde(range(min = 1, max = 10))]
  value: u32,
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#rule-adapters)Rule adapters

Adapters allow you to implement validation for third-party types without using a newtype.

An adapter may look like this:

```
mod my_str_adapter {
    #![allow(unused_imports)]
    pub use garde::rules::*; // re-export garde's rules
    pub mod length {
        pub use garde::rules::length::*; // re-export `length` rules
        pub mod simple {
            // re-implement `simple`, but _only_ for the concrete type &str!
            pub fn apply(v: &str, (min, max): (usize, usize)) -> garde::Result {
                if !(min..=max).contains(&v.len()) {
                    Err(garde::Error::new("my custom error message"))
                } else {
                    Ok(())
                }
            }
        }
    }
}
```
You create a module, add a public glob re-export of `garde::rules` inside of it,
and then re-implement the specific rule you’re interested in. This is a form of
[duck typing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duck_typing). Any rule which you have
not re-implemented is simply delegated to `garde`’s impl.

It’s quite verbose, but in exchange it is maximally flexible. To use the adapter,
add an `adapt` attribute to a field:

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
#[derive(garde::Validate)]
struct Stuff<'a> {
    #[garde(
        adapt(my_str_adapter),
        length(min = 1),
        ascii,
    )]
    v: &'a str,
}
```
The `length` rule will now use your custom implementation, but the `ascii` rule
will continue to use `garde`’s implementation.

[§](https://docs.rs#integration-with-web-frameworks)Integration with web frameworks

[§](https://docs.rs#feature-flags)Feature flags

| name | description | extra dependencies |
|---|---|---|
| `derive` | Enables the usage of the `derive(Validate)`macro | `garde_derive` |
| `url` | Validation of URLs via the `url`crate. | `url` |
| `email` | Validation of emails according to [HTML5](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/forms.html#valid-e-mail-address) | ,`regex``once_cell` |
| `email-idna` | Support for [Internationalizing Domain Names for Applications](https://url.spec.whatwg.org/#idna)in email addresses | `idna` |
| `regex` | Support for regular expressions in `pattern`via the`regex`crate | ,`regex``once_cell` |
| `credit-card` | Validation of credit card numbers via the `card-validate`crate | `card-validate` |
| `phone-number` | Validation of phone numbers via the `phonenumber`crate | `phonenumber` |
| `unicode` | Validation of grapheme count via the `unicode-segmentation`crate | `unicode-segmentation` |

[§](https://docs.rs#why-garde)Why `garde`?

Garde means guard in French. I am not French, nor do I speak the language, but `guard` was taken, and this is close enough :).

# valid_ymd in facett_form - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/facett-form/0.1.10/facett_form/fn.valid_ymd.html

## Expand description

Validate `YYYY-MM-DD` cheaply (no date crate): four-digit year, 01–12 month,
01–31 day (day-in-month not range-checked beyond 31). Handy as a garde
`#[garde(custom(facett_form::valid_ymd))]` rule for [ FormUi::date](https://docs.rs/struct.FormUi.html#method.date) fields.

# facett_filedialog - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/facett-filedialog/0.1.10/target-redirect/facett_filedialog/

## Expand description

**facett-filedialog** (§21) — a **themed, in-app** file dialog (native `rfd`
dialogs can’t be themed, so we draw a coherent one in egui). Open / open-many /
save / pick-folder, fully keyboard-navigable via the shared [`KeyMap`]
(arrows = move, `Confirm`/`Cancel`, type-to-filter, `Copy` a path). It is a
[ Facet](https://docs.rs/facett-core/0.1.10/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/facett_core/trait.Facet.html) (picturable headlessly with an

**injected listing**— FILE-3) and composes with §5 (open as a glass overlay).

The listing is **injected** (`set_entries`), not read from disk, so the dialog
is deterministic + testable; a host wires real `std::fs` reads to `set_entries`
as an effect. FILE-2 (optional native `rfd` backend) is a host-side feature.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Entry](https://docs.rs/struct.Entry.html)
- One listing entry (injected).
- [File](https://docs.rs/struct.FileDialog.html)- Dialog
- The themed file dialog. All observable state lives here (FC-1); the listing is
injected (`set_entries`) so it renders deterministically headless (FILE-3).

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Dialog](https://docs.rs/enum.DialogMode.html)- Mode
- What the dialog is for (FILE-1).
- [Outcome](https://docs.rs/enum.Outcome.html)
- What the dialog resolved to when the user confirmed.

# FileDialog in facett_filedialog - Rust

`pub struct FileDialog { /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

The themed file dialog. All observable state lives here (FC-1); the listing is
injected (`set_entries`) so it renders deterministically headless (FILE-3).

# rayon - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/rayon/^1/

## Expand description

Rayon is a data-parallelism library that makes it easy to convert sequential computations into parallel.

It is lightweight and convenient for introducing parallelism into existing code. It guarantees data-race free executions and takes advantage of parallelism when sensible, based on work-load at runtime.

[§](https://docs.rs#how-to-use-rayon)How to use Rayon

There are two ways to use Rayon:

- **High-level parallel constructs**are the simplest way to use Rayon and also typically the most efficient.- [Parallel iterators](https://docs.rs/iter/index.html)make it easy to convert a sequential iterator to execute in parallel.- The `ParallelIterator`
- The `IndexedParallelIterator`

- The
- The `par_sort``&mut [T]`slices (or vectors) in parallel.
- `par_extend`

- **Custom tasks**let you divide your work into parallel tasks yourself.- `join`
- `scope`
- `ThreadPoolBuilder`

[§](https://docs.rs#basic-usage-and-the-rayon-prelude)Basic usage and the Rayon prelude

First, you will need to add `rayon` to your `Cargo.toml`.

Next, to use parallel iterators or the other high-level methods,
you need to import several traits. Those traits are bundled into
the module [ rayon::prelude](https://docs.rs/prelude/index.html). It is recommended that you import
all of these traits at once by adding

`use rayon::prelude::*` at
the top of each module that uses Rayon methods.These traits give you access to the `par_iter` method which provides
parallel implementations of many iterative functions such as [ map](https://docs.rs/iter/trait.ParallelIterator.html#method.map),

[,](https://docs.rs/iter/trait.ParallelIterator.html#method.for_each)

`for_each`[,](https://docs.rs/iter/trait.ParallelIterator.html#method.filter)

`filter`[, and](https://docs.rs/iter/trait.ParallelIterator.html#method.fold)

`fold`[more](https://docs.rs/iter/trait.ParallelIterator.html#provided-methods).

[§](https://docs.rs#crate-layout)Crate Layout

Rayon extends many of the types found in the standard library with
parallel iterator implementations. The modules in the `rayon`
crate mirror [ std](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/index.html) itself: so, e.g., the

`option` module in
Rayon contains parallel iterators for the `Option` type, which is
found in [the](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/index.html). Similarly, the

`option` module of `std``collections` module in Rayon offers parallel iterator types for
[the](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/collections/index.html). You will rarely need to access these submodules unless you need to name iterator types explicitly.

`collections` from `std`[§](https://docs.rs#targets-without-threading)Targets without threading

Rayon has limited support for targets without `std` threading implementations.
See the [ rayon_core](https://docs.rs/rayon-core/1.13.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/rayon_core/index.html) documentation for more information about its global fallback.

[§](https://docs.rs#other-questions)Other questions?

See [the Rayon FAQ](https://github.com/rayon-rs/rayon/blob/main/FAQ.md).

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Broadcast](https://docs.rs/struct.BroadcastContext.html)- Context
- Provides context to a closure called by `broadcast`.
- [FnContext](https://docs.rs/struct.FnContext.html)
- Provides the calling context to a closure called by `join_context`.
- [Scope](https://docs.rs/struct.Scope.html)
- Represents a fork-join scope which can be used to spawn any number of tasks.
See `scope()`
- [Scope](https://docs.rs/struct.ScopeFifo.html)- Fifo
- Represents a fork-join scope which can be used to spawn any number of tasks.
Those spawned from the same thread are prioritized in relative FIFO order.
See `scope_fifo()`
- [Thread](https://docs.rs/struct.ThreadBuilder.html)- Builder
- Thread builder used for customization via `ThreadPoolBuilder::spawn_handler()`
- [Thread](https://docs.rs/struct.ThreadPool.html)- Pool
- Represents a user-created [thread pool](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thread_pool).
- [Thread](https://docs.rs/struct.ThreadPoolBuildError.html)- Pool - Build - Error
- Error when initializing a thread pool.
- [Thread](https://docs.rs/struct.ThreadPoolBuilder.html)- Pool - Builder
- Used to create a new `ThreadPool`
